answer_1.quote: We propose Collaborative STORM (Co-STORM), an information-seeking assistance system that supports collaborative discourse among users and multiple LM agents... Upon the conclusion of the discourse, users can request the system to generate a cited report based on the mind map.
answer_1.outputs: Long-form cited reports and turn-based discourse utterances

answer_2.quote: We propose automatic metrics to assess both discourse trace and final report quality... Report Quality We evaluate the final report on four aspects, Relevance, Broad Coverage (Breadth), Depth, and Novelty... Discourse Quality Since the discourse itself is valuable for human learning, we also evaluate the discourse trace using a 5-point rubric... We also report the number of unique cited URLs in these utterances to indicate information diversity at the turn level.

answer_3.quote: We employ Prometheus, an open‑source rubric grading model, to score the report based on a 5‑point rubric... To assess the quality of the automatic evaluation results... we calculate the Pearson correlation between the automatic evaluation scores and the average human grading scores.
methods: LLM‑based rubric grading via zero‑shot prompts

answer_4.quote: We conduct an IRB‑approved human evaluation to compare Co-STORM with a search engine and a RAG chatbot by recruiting 20 volunteers... Participants are asked to seek information on two topics... After seeking information for each topic, participants are instructed to rate their experience based on four grading aspects defined in §5.2 (Relevance, Breadth, Depth, Novelty/Serendipity), using a 5‑point Likert scale... participants were asked to provide pairwise preferences regarding the required effort, user engagement, addressing echo chamber issues, and overall experience.
answer_4.guideline: Rate each system on a 5‑point Likert scale for Relevance, Breadth, Depth, Serendipity and answer pairwise preference questions on effort, engagement, echo‑chamber mitigation, and overall experience.
